# The Cycle Raises the Bar


October 1, 2026


[Calamos Growth and Income Fund (CGIIX)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/mutual/growth-and-income-cgiix/)


[John Hillenbrand](https://www.calamos.com/about/investment-organization/john-hillenbrand/) , CPA


***Summary Points:***


- We have moved to a positive but more cautious risk posture; the mid-cycle expansion is running ahead of our July base case, and the Fed has begun raising rates to catch up with it.
- As inflation stalled above target and the Fed began raising rates, we reduced risk by adding index puts, paring equity-like convertibles, and shifting toward less cyclical sectors and factors, while keeping our equity overweight.
- Earnings broadened this year as we expected, but consensus expectations see 2027 growth re-concentrating in technology; higher rates raise the bar, and new positions must show growth in both revenue and margins.
- AI remains the earnings engine; we have shifted some of our exposure toward the platforms and software that monetize it and away from the capital-spending supply chain.
- We would de-risk further if rates rose on risk premia rather than a higher neutral rate, if AI financing tightened, if hyperscaler spending guidance were cut, or if labor market data broke decisively.


## Calamos Growth and Income Fund (CGIIX)


** ** ** ** ** Morningstar Overall RatingTM Among 116 Moderately Aggressive Allocation funds. The Fund's risk-adjusted returns based on load-waived Class I Shares had 4 stars for 3 years, 4 stars for 5 years and 5 stars for 10 years out of 116, 111 and 97 Moderately Aggressive Allocation Funds, respectively, for the period ended 8/31/2026.


The US economy remains in a mid-cycle expansion, running ahead of the base case we set out in July. Tracking estimates put third-quarter growth near 2.75%, earnings growth has broadened across the market, and investment tied to artificial intelligence remains the largest single source of real growth. The forces against the expansion have also grown: inflation has stalled above target; the Strait of Hormuz remains contested with Brent crude near $100, and Houthi forces now threaten the Red Sea route around it; and policy moves on Iran, Russia, and tariffs have weighed on growth. The Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 basis points in September to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, its first increase since 2023, and its projections point to one more this year. The question this quarter is why rates are rising. We believe it is because the cycle is strong enough to lift the neutral rate, not because policy is tightening into a slowdown. We have moved to a positive but more cautious risk posture.


Last quarter, we asked whether that shock was large enough to end the expansion or whether it was a disruption the cycle could absorb. It was the latter. The question now is different. It is not whether the cycle survives a shock but whether its leadership broadens beyond a narrow set of AI winners or remains concentrated. We expect broadening. Growth is holding near 2%, headline inflation is elevated but moderating, the labor market is softening but not breaking, and the earnings growth that has carried the market is beginning to widen.


[Our July outlook](https://www.calamos.com/blogs/voices/broadening-earnings-growth-broadening-opportunities/) expected leadership to broaden beyond a narrow set of AI winners, inflation to moderate steadily, and the rate path to remain too uncertain to position around. Earnings broadened; prices did not. Inflation stalled above target instead, and the rate uncertainty resolved toward hikes.


[Calamos Growth and Income Fund (CGIIX)](https://www.calamos.com/funds/mutual/growth-and-income-cgiix/) returned 0.46% for the quarter, behind the S&P 500 Index’s 2.30% and ahead of the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index’s −3.51%. Our overweight in equity exposure relative to fixed income added value; where we held it did not. The quarter’s momentum leaders in the AI capital-spending supply chain and electrification reversed as rates rose and concerns over data centers and AI safety weighed on sentiment. Our overweight there was the largest detractor, along with the cost of index protection, while positions in AI platforms, software, and refiners contributed. Convertibles cushioned part of the decline, except where they had become equity-like, and we have shifted out of those positions into new issues with more balanced attributes.


## Growth Drivers Remain Intact


The positive forces supporting economic expansion are still intact. Fiscal support continues to flow, the deregulatory impulse is additive to growth, and hyperscaler capital spending guidance has continued to ratchet higher. We expect AI spending to prove largely resilient to higher rates because demand remains strong and the largest spenders are competing for market share. Frontier AI models improved substantially again this quarter, and as pricing moves from flat fees to usage-based billing, customers are paying for more usage, which we interpret as evidence that the models return real value to users. Many of the current model capabilities are still underused, and companies are only now building the software harnesses that connect the models to their own data and workflows, which is where capability turns into productivity.


Our highest-conviction view is that adoption is in its early stages. We interpret the selloff in the AI capital-spending supply chain as driven more by sentiment than fundamentals. Concerns over data centers and AI safety intensified even as use cases broadened, and in September, semiconductor shares rebounded while technology earnings estimates kept rising. Developers are addressing local concerns over power costs and community impact, including pledges to pay for their own electricity, and we expect those concerns to ease after the November elections. AI safety is a legitimate concern, but it’s one we believe the industry can address.


Earnings breadth is less secure than it looks. Consensus estimates place most of next year’s index earnings growth in technology, and the slowdown elsewhere largely reflects margins and the lapping of one-time investment gains, although revenue growth also slows in most sectors. That is where the bar rises. Outside AI, we now require growth in both revenue and margins, with real growth tailwinds and improving returns on capital to back it.

## Rates and the Inflation Question


The forces weighing against the expansion are real but, in our assessment, manageable. Since February, the 10-year Treasury yield has risen more than a full point to its highest level since 2002, almost entirely in real yields, while inflation expectations have held steady. We interpret this as a higher neutral rate, with strong growth and the capital demands of the AI buildout, which Fed Chair Warsh has cited, lifting real rates globally alongside fiscal deficits. As the neutral rate rises, a given policy rate becomes less restrictive. Higher rates may slow growth at the margin, but we do not expect them to substantially increase recession risk at this time. They do raise the discount rate on the longest-duration equity and the hurdle that every investment must clear. The most recent interest rate increases coincided with a global bond selloff driven by increased growth expectations. We would be concerned if rates rose higher on worries about government borrowing rather than on economic strength.

## Positioning and Outlook


Our positioning reflects this framework. In July, we said we would de-risk through the convertible and options sleeves if inflation re-accelerated and the Fed turned decisively toward hikes. Inflation stalled rather than re-accelerated, but the Fed raised rates nonetheless. Because higher policy rates weigh most on our longest-duration holdings, we decided to reduce risk. We added index puts to mitigate exposure to equity drawdowns, sold convertibles that had become equity-like, redeployed assets into balanced new issues with more convexity, and shifted sector and factor exposure toward less cyclical and less risky areas. We reduced exposure to industrials and the capital-spending supply chain, where our caution concerns valuation rather than demand, and added to health care, where new product introductions and improving margins offer real growth tailwinds and improving returns on capital into 2027. Consensus expects health care earnings to grow about 22% next year, second only to technology.


We also added short-term Treasuries and lower-beta income exposure, and we hold energy close to benchmark weight on the view that supply and demand adjust over the intermediate term. Under US naval escort, crude flows through the Strait have recovered to prewar levels, and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are pushing back against the Houthis, though record tanker rates and constrained refinery output are keeping fuel prices high. We did not move to a defensive posture and kept our equity overweight, consistent with our view that the hike reflects a higher neutral rate rather than restriction.


**Base case (highest probability).** The expansion continues above trend in the near term and moderates toward the low 2% range into 2027. The Fed follows a higher neutral rate with one or two further increases rather than a sustained cycle. Core inflation holds near 3%, and oil eases as supply and demand adjust, leaving returns dependent on earnings rather than multiples.


**Upside case.** The Strait reopens under a negotiated settlement, disinflation accelerates, and AI monetization outpaces spending, lowering the hurdle for returns on capital.


**Downside case.** Yields rise on risk premia rather than a higher neutral rate, or faster than equities can absorb, or tighter AI financing stalls the spending cycle even with demand intact.


Third-quarter earnings and hyperscaler guidance, inflation and the Fed, the Strait of Hormuz, and the US November elections will determine which path materializes. We would de-risk further if rates rose on risk premia, AI spending or financing weakened, or labor data broke, and would add on cleaner inflation and broader earnings growth. The cycle is now strong enough to raise the bar, and we are positioned to own the businesses that clear it.
